text: What happens with my body during coronavirus?

steps.title: The virus gets in
steps.say: As an example, this copy has you two days into COVID. The virus lands in your nose and airways and latches onto a doorway protein called ACE2 to get inside lining cells.

composed.caption: Coronavirus entering airway lining cells
composed.basis: Textbook picture of SARS-CoV-2 binding ACE2 on airway cells (Hoffmann et al. 2020); amounts are illustration

steps.title: Airways get sore
steps.say: Infected cells make copies and call for help, so the lining swells and gets irritated. That's the sore throat, stuffy nose and the cough trying to clear it.

steps.title: Immune army and fever
steps.say: Immune cells pour out of the blood toward the virus, and their signals turn up your thermostat. Your temperature here is about 37.9 °C, which slows the virus down.

steps.title: Heart works harder
steps.say: A hotter body burns more fuel, and the heart beats roughly 8 to 9 beats faster per degree of fever. You're near 88 at rest right now.

steps.title: Sugar handling slips
steps.say: Inflammation makes your cells answer insulin weakly, so your pizza's sugar lingers in the blood longer and your pancreas has to push out more insulin.

steps.title: Why you feel wiped
steps.say: Those same immune signals reach the brain and make you tired, achy and off your food. It's the body saving energy for the fight, and sweating drains fluid too.

lines.text: The virus gets into your airway lining cells, and immune cells rush in to fight it.
That fight brings fever, cough, sore throat and a faster heart, about 88 here.
You may feel drained and lose your appetite, because immune signals reach your brain too.
